analysis.one_liner: Lets people wipe out private student loans in bankruptcy like almost any other debt.
analysis.headline: The bill has sat in the House Judiciary Committee since January 2025 with no hearing, no vote, and no movement.
analysis.plain_summary: Right now, nearly all student loans can be erased in bankruptcy only if you prove the debt causes 'undue hardship' — a standard so strict that most borrowers never even try. This bill lifts that rule for private student loans (the ones from banks and lenders, not federal loans), so people buried in that debt could discharge it in bankruptcy like credit card debt or medical bills. It applies to new bankruptcy cases filed after the bill takes effect.
analysis.who_benefits: People drowning in private student loan debt — often those who attended for-profit or vocational schools and were not eligible for federal protections — would regain the same access to a financial fresh start that people with credit card or medical debt have. Former borrowers who lost a job, became disabled, or were misled by a school could have the debt wiped out instead of paying it for decades.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Borrowers stuck with private student loans

how_it_helps.text: The bill removes the 'undue hardship' requirement for private student loans, letting them be discharged in bankruptcy like other consumer debts [S2][S3].

Under current law, a borrower must file a separate lawsuit within their bankruptcy and prove that repaying the loans would prevent them from maintaining a minimal standard of living — a test so hard to meet that many borrowers never attempt a discharge [S2].
The change applies to bankruptcy cases filed after enactment, so it would immediately benefit newly filing borrowers rather than a delayed group [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Private student loan lenders would lose their guaranteed protection against bankruptcy discharge, meaning more unpaid balances and potentially higher interest rates or tighter lending standards on future private student loans.

drawbacks.text: Lenders argue that without the bankruptcy shield they would charge higher interest rates or lend less, particularly to students at schools with weak outcomes, because defaults could be erased in bankruptcy [S2] (current-law context) — this is the standard industry objection to restoring pre-2005 rules.
The bill covers only private student loans; federal student loans would still require an undue hardship showing, so the majority of borrowers in distress would not benefit [S2][S3].

A borrower who successfully discharges a private loan shifts the loss to the lender's other customers and shareholders, and loosened dischargeability could also let some borrowers who could repay walk away from the debt.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and targeted: it restores a bankruptcy right for a class of borrowers who currently face one of the harshest discharge standards in law. The main cost is that lenders may price that risk into future loans, making private student credit somewhat more expensive. On balance, the bill trades a modest, uncertain cost in credit pricing for a significant fresh-start right for people already in financial ruin — the standard tradeoff bankruptcy law makes for every other kind of consumer debt.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee has taken no action on it since.

narrative.text: Rep. Steve Cohen introduced the bill on January 15, 2025, with four original cosponsors [S3].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary [S5].
No further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — appears in the action history [S5].
The bill has 5 cosponsors, all Democrats [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private student loan lenders, who keep the current-law protection that makes their loans nearly impossible to erase in bankruptcy, and no one else — the bill has simply gone nowhere.

sides.party_line_note: All six House supporters in the record are Democrats; no Republican cosponsors appear, and the bill sits in committee without action [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Private student loan lenders and servicers
industries.note: The bill strips the special bankruptcy protection that keeps private student loans collectible even when a borrower's finances collapse. Its interest in the bill runs against distressed borrowers, who would regain the right to discharge the debt.

industries.industry: Debt collectors and student loan servicers
industries.note: Debts erased in bankruptcy cannot be pursued further, shrinking the pool of old private student loan balances available for collection.

Restoring straightforward dischargeability of private student loans expands the caseload of straightforward consumer bankruptcies and removes the expensive adversary litigation the hardship test requires.

analysis.trajectory: With only five cosponsors, no committee action in months, and no hearing scheduled, the bill is very likely to sit in the Judiciary Committee until the 119th Congress ends without a vote — the same path similar private-loan discharge bills have followed in past Congresses.
